name: Italian Renaissance Revival

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor: the fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Florentine and Roman palazzo, reached through measured plates and photographs rather than through any continuous practice.
Villa parti, arcaded loggia and window aedicule; the villa subtype quotes Palladio directly.
The true descent. Same offices - McKim, Mead & White above all - same draughting room, same clients, differing chiefly in restraint.
Ecole composition and the analytique exercise, which trained the eye that reads a palazzo elevation as a stacked order problem.
The American Victorian palazzo habit - bracketed cornice, round-arched openings, low hipped roof - persisting in builder practice and re-academicised after 1890.
The Villard Houses of 1882-84 are an explicit rebuke of Romanesque weight and rustication in favour of a flat, correct, planar palazzo wall.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The academic American palazzo: a symmetrical masonry block with a low tile-hipped roof, a heavy bracketed or modillioned cornice, differentiated storeys with arcaded openings below and diminishing windows above, built as the sober alternative to Beaux-Arts display.
description.long:
Italian Renaissance Revival begins in 1882 on Madison Avenue, when Joseph Morrill Wells of McKim, Mead & White persuaded his partners to abandon a picturesque scheme for the Villard Houses and instead build a flat-walled palazzo modelled on the Cancelleria in Rome. The building was a professional event. It demonstrated that an American commercial-scale residence could be composed as a single planar block of correctly-proportioned storeys, and it made the palazzo the default for anyone who wanted to appear cultivated rather than merely rich. For fifty years afterwards the same formula was applied to town houses, country villas, clubs, banks, libraries and apartment buildings.

The grammar is compact and unusually rule-bound. The block is symmetrical and rectangular; the roof is low-pitched and hipped, tiled in red or green, with a wide overhang on brackets; the wall is treated as a plane and its storeys are differentiated in the Renaissance manner, so that the ground floor is heavier - rusticated, arcaded, or both - and each storey above it is lighter and shorter, with windows diminishing in height and elaboration as they rise. Openings are round-arched at the ground and rectangular above, often within aedicules of pilasters and pediment. A string course marks each floor. The entrance is recessed under an arch. This system is genuinely proportional in a way Colonial Revival's is not: change the ground storey height and everything above it must change.

What produced it, beyond the Ecole training that produced the whole family, was a specific economic fact - the arrival in America of the professional stone contractor and of terra cotta as a mass-produced substitute for carved stone. Terra cotta could deliver a modillioned cornice, an aedicule, and a full arcade at a fraction of the cost of carving, and it is the reason the style spread from Vanderbilt-scale town houses to speculative apartment blocks in Chicago and Kansas City within twenty years. The buyers were the American haute bourgeoisie - bankers, publishers, professionals - who wanted Renaissance associations for exactly the reasons a Medici would have recognised: mercantile wealth seeking the legitimacy of learning.

A good Italian Renaissance Revival building is calm to the point of severity, and its calm is what people remember. The wall is flat and cool, jointed finely, with no projection except the cornice, and the cornice is enormous - four to six feet of overhang throwing a hard black shadow across the top of the building on any sunny day. The windows sit in the wall rather than on it. There is no picturesque incident anywhere; nothing overhangs, nothing turns a corner, nothing surprises. Standing beneath the cornice on a bright afternoon and looking up into that band of shadow is the whole aesthetic experience the style has to offer, and it is a genuinely good one.

defining_characteristics: Symmetrical rectangular masonry block treated as a planar wall, with no picturesque projection
Low-pitched hipped roof, 3:12 to 5:12, covered in clay tile, often not visible from the street on urban examples
A heavy projecting cornice on modillions or brackets, with an overhang of substantial depth relative to the wall
Storey differentiation in the Renaissance manner: heavier and taller at the ground, progressively lighter and shorter above, with string courses marking each floor
Round-arched openings and/or an arcaded loggia at the ground storey, rectangular openings above, frequently within pilastered aedicules
Recessed entrance under an arch, on the centre line, without a projecting portico
diagnostic_tells: Storey heights diminish upward and windows shrink with them. Colonial and Neoclassical Revival keep storey heights nearly equal and windows identical between floors.
The cornice overhang is 1/12 to 1/16 of the total wall height and is carried on visible modillions - much deeper than any Colonial Revival cornice and much plainer than any Beaux-Arts one.
No portico and no columns in front of the wall. The order, where present, is engaged as pilasters within the wall plane.
Tile roof plus a symmetrical flat-walled block plus arched ground-floor openings. Take away the symmetry and the arcade wraps a courtyard, and it becomes Mediterranean Revival.

Compared with the Italian original: the revival has plate glass, an even and generous fenestration, no ground-floor shops, no rustication above the first storey, and a service plan behind the piano nobile that no palazzo had.

distinguished_from.difference: Italianate, 1840-1885, is a wood or brick Victorian type with a square tower, tall thin round-arched windows with elaborate hoods, and a bracketed cornice that is scaled to a house rather than to a palace. Italian Renaissance Revival is academically proportioned, masonry, and treats the wall as a plane.

Mediterranean Revival is looser, warmer, and organised around outdoor rooms - loggias, courtyards, terraces, arcaded galleries - with rougher stucco and asymmetrical extension. Italian Renaissance Revival is a formal symmetrical block whose exterior spaces, if any, are subordinate.

The original palazzo is a fortified urban courtyard building with a blind or barred ground storey, a cortile as the only source of light to the interior rooms, and 3-4 ft masonry walls. The revival opens the ground floor with an arcaded loggia, glazes generously, and plans on American corridor logic.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The stacked classical order in the Renaissance manner. A nominal order governs each storey, the orders diminish upward in the canonical sequence, and the cornice is proportioned to the full height of the building rather than to the top storey.
typical_ratios: Storey heights descending roughly 1.0 : 0.85 : 0.7 from ground to third
Cornice projection 1/12 to 1/16 of total wall height; on a 40 ft wall, 30-40 in.
Window openings 1:1.8 to 1:2.2 at the ground storey, tightening to 1:1.5 at the top
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 in barrel or pan-and-cover clay tile
Arcade piers 1/3 to 1/2 of the clear arch span; arch springing at 2/3 of opening height
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Strictly even, three to nine bays, with all bays equal except where a centre bay is widened for the entrance arch. Vertical alignment between storeys is absolute - unlike every picturesque style in this family, a single misaligned window is visible from across the street.

massing_affinities.note: The suburban and country version: a symmetrical double-pile block under a low tile hip.
Villa examples with a loggia on the garden side and service wings returning.
The literal palazzo case, a full cortile, as at Vizcaya.
Where the villa subtype is taken directly from Palladio.
The reduced builder version, 1905-1925: a hipped tile-roofed cube with a bracketed cornice and an arched entry.

constraints.statement: Storey heights must diminish upward. Second-storey clear height not more than 90 percent of the first, third not more than 85 percent of the second. Equal storey heights place the building in Colonial or Neoclassical Revival.

test.note: Tests the second-to-first storey diminishment (clear height <=90% of the first, i.e. >=10% reduction). The third-to-second pair (<=85%, >=15% reduction) is the same variable applied one storey pair further up and stays prose, per the corpus's established multi-storey-diminishment pattern.

constraints.statement: Cornice projection not less than 1/16 of total wall height and not less than 24 in. on any two-storey example, carried on modillions or brackets spaced 12-24 in. on centre. A cornice under 12 in. voids the style.

test.note: Tests the absolute 24in floor for a two-storey example. The proportional alternative (not less than 1/16 of total wall height) and bracket/modillion spacing (12-24in o.c.) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12, clay tile only, with no gable facing any principal elevation. Asphalt shingle, or any pitch above 6:12, is forbidden.

test.note: Material (clay tile only) and 'no gable facing any principal elevation' stay prose.

constraints.statement: Masonry walls must express thickness at openings with a minimum 6 in. reveal, and arches must be true arches with visible voussoirs or a moulded archivolt - not flat headers behind a stucco curve.

test.note: Arch construction (true voussoirs/archivolt vs. a flat header behind a stucco curve) is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No projecting portico or free-standing column in front of the wall plane. Where an order is used it must be engaged as a pilaster with a projection not exceeding 1/6 of its width.

exemplars.name: Villard Houses
exemplars.location: 451 Madison Avenue, New York, New York
exemplars.note: Joseph Morrill Wells for McKim, Mead & White, after the Palazzo della Cancelleria in Rome. The founding building of the style in America.
exemplars.why: The node's own prose opens with it -- 'Italian Renaissance Revival begins in 1882 on Madison Avenue' -- and the HABS sheet caption says why: 'Appearing as a single Italian palazzo, the Villard Houses were actually six residences built around a central courtyard.'

exemplars.name: Boston Public Library, McKim Building
exemplars.note: McKim, Mead & White. Not domestic, but the clearest demonstration of the arcaded palazzo wall as a compositional system.
exemplars.why: The node's own exemplar note: not domestic, 'but the clearest demonstration of the arcaded palazzo wall as a compositional system'; a National Historic Landmark since 1986 (Wikipedia).

exemplars.name: The Breakers
exemplars.note: Richard Morris Hunt for Cornelius Vanderbilt II, on a sixteenth-century Genoese palazzo model. The style at maximum budget, where it overlaps Beaux-Arts.
exemplars.why: The node's own note calls it 'the style at maximum budget, where it overlaps Beaux-Arts', and the HABS data page measures that budget: about 250 x 150 ft, thirteen stone chimneys, a steel lattice frame.

exemplars.name: Vizcaya
exemplars.note: F. Burrall Hoffman with Paul Chalfin. Veneto villa parti around a true cortile; the point where Italian Renaissance Revival and Mediterranean Revival separate.
exemplars.why: The point where the node says Italian Renaissance Revival and Mediterranean Revival separate, and the register agrees: Wikipedia's style line reads 'Mediterranean Revival Style; with Baroque, Italian Renaissance, Italian Renaissance Revival'.

exemplars.name: Henry Clay Frick House
exemplars.location: 1 East 70th Street, New York, New York
exemplars.note: Thomas Hastings of Carrère and Hastings, 1913-14: a single-family palazzo on a full Fifth Avenue block front, built low on purpose and now the Frick Collection. National Historic Landmark 2008; the city landmark designation covers the facade only.
exemplars.why: The Register lists it as an NHL (Wikipedia infobox, 08001091, 2008) and it is the palazzo formula at domestic scale on the avenue where the node says the buyers lived.

exemplars.name: University Club of New York
exemplars.location: 1 West 54th Street, New York, New York
exemplars.note: McKim, Mead and White, 1899: nine storeys composed as a three-storey Florentine palazzo, each great storey holding a mezzanine, on a corner of Fifth Avenue. The proportional system the node describes -- change the ground storey and everything above must change -- run at its largest scale.
exemplars.why: The node's own prose names clubs among the formula's applications, and the Register (80002726, 1980) and the city (landmark 0263, 1967) both list this one.

exemplars.name: Payne Whitney House
exemplars.location: 972 Fifth Avenue, New York, New York
exemplars.note: Stanford White, completed 1909, on a 45 ft frontage: a bowed granite town house 'in the High Italian Renaissance style', among the last houses White designed before 1906, and since 1952 the French embassy's cultural services. New York City landmark 1970.
exemplars.why: Wikipedia records it as designed 'in the High Italian Renaissance style by architect Stanford White', and it is the node's formula at row-house width rather than block scale.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Leland M. Roth, McKim, Mead & White, Architects (1983)
Richard Guy Wilson, The American Renaissance 1876-1917 (1979)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)

proportion_packs.note: Takes the geometry from its parent and states it in the same terms -- 'arcade piers 1/3 to 1/2 of the clear arch span; arch springing at 2/3 of opening height' -- which is one of the three records the springing rule rests on. Bound facade: this record puts the arcaded loggia at the ground storey with rectangular openings above, so the arcade is the base of the elevation rather than a courtyard, and `storey-graduation`, already bound here, governs what sits on it.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, which names italian-renaissance-revival directly alongside beaux-arts-american. Bound plain rather than as a Chambers, Gibbs or Palladio overlay, per the batch guidance's steer toward whichever base reading is genuinely period-correct: the style's own diagnostic tells insist the order, 'where present, is engaged as pilasters within the wall plane' rather than free-standing or porticoed, and pilaster orders on the piano nobile of an American palazzo (Villard Houses, the Boston Public Library) are the register Corinthian or Composite pilasters occupy in the real Roman and Florentine palazzi this style claims as ancestor. Corinthian rather than Composite because the style is explicitly the 'sober alternative' to Beaux-Arts display (see distinguished_from) and Corinthian is the lighter, less imperial of the two rich orders.

JUDGMENT BINDING: not confirmed in vignola-doric's own applies_to for this specific node, but general and typological rather than fabricated - the stacked-order palazzo convention (sturdy order at the rusticated ground storey, lighter and richer orders rising) is the ordinary Renaissance grammar Serlio and Alberti both describe and every American Beaux-Arts-trained office inherited. The style's own defining_characteristics call for a ground storey 'heavier - rusticated, arcaded, or both' under a lighter principal storey above; Doric is the order the rest of this corpus consistently assigns to the heaviest, plainest register (see the Georgian template's own doric-for-the-everyday-order note), which is the honest general reasoning this pairing rests on.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs bay count and solid-to-void, though the style's own hard constraint that storey heights must diminish (c01, second not more than 90 percent of the first) is stricter than facade-classical's own default graduation and is better read through storey-graduation below.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Covers the rectangular openings of the upper storeys directly; the round-arched ground-storey openings and arcaded loggia the style's defining_characteristics call for are a further elaboration this pack does not itself model and are covered qualitatively by the style's own constraint c04 (true arches, minimum 6 in reveal).

JUDGMENT BINDING: this specific id is absent from trim-classical's own applies_to list, though the sibling id renaissance-revival-american is present there - almost certainly a curation gap rather than a deliberate exclusion, since nothing about this style's interiors (stacked orders, string courses, a wall read as a classical order) argues against the family and everything argues for it over trim-craftsman, which is not in contention here at all.

JUDGMENT BINDING: this specific id is likewise absent from storey-graduation's own applies_to list (again, renaissance-revival-american is present but not this id), yet the style's own proportional_system states the diminution almost as a paraphrase of the pack's own derived rules - 'Storey heights descending roughly 1.0 : 0.85 : 0.7 from ground to third' against the pack's 0.85-then-0.80 compounding, which resolves to 0.85 : 0.68. The two are close enough that this is a documented near-match, not a fabricated one, and the small numeric gap (0.7 stated vs 0.68 derived) is worth carrying forward rather than silently reconciling.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to.
